subject: Agriculture
title: Subsidies and Farm Policy
description: A quick, practical guide to Subsidies and Farm Policy.

hook.text: American corn sells for less than it costs to grow. The government pays the difference—every year.

buildup.text: Farm subsidies began during the Great Depression to prevent farmer bankruptcies and stabilize food supply.

discovery.text: Today, rich nations spend over $700 billion annually subsidizing agriculture. Most goes to large operations.

twist.text: Cheap subsidized exports undercut farmers in developing countries who can't compete on price.

climax.text: Subsidies shape what gets grown. Corn and soy dominate because that's where the money flows.

punchline.text: Governments don't just regulate farming. They design it.

quiz.question: How much do rich nations spend annually on agricultural subsidies?

details.summary: Government subsidies and farm policies have shaped agriculture since the Great Depression. This topic covers the origins of farm support programs, how they influence what gets grown, and the ongoing debate about whether subsidies help or harm food systems.
details.whyItMatters: Farm policies determine crop prices, land use, and rural livelihoods for millions. Understanding their history reveals why modern food systems overproduce commodity crops while underinvesting in nutrition.
takeaways: US farm subsidies originated in the New Deal to rescue Depression-era farmers
The EU's Common Agricultural Policy consumes about one-third of the EU budget
Subsidies disproportionately benefit large farms growing commodity crops

faq.question: Why were farm subsidies originally created?
faq.answer: Farm subsidies were introduced during the Great Depression to prevent farm bankruptcies, stabilize food prices, and ensure a reliable food supply. The US Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1933 paid farmers to reduce production and raise prices.

faq.question: How do farm subsidies affect what food is produced?
faq.answer: Subsidies for corn, wheat, soy, and other commodities make these crops artificially profitable, encouraging overproduction. This keeps processed food ingredients cheap while fruits, vegetables, and diverse crops receive far less support.
